extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners (PR professionals, communicators, media relations specialists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for developing action programs and crafting message content and delivery in public relations, including crisis response, framing, newsworthiness, semantics, and encoding/decoding considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrective action addresses root cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Action is necessary to eliminate the original source of the problem (example: university gave freshmen registration priority to restore enrollment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take concrete organizational actions that remove the underlying cause rather than relying solely on communication; measure effectiveness by whether the source of the problem is eliminated and desired outcomes (e.g., increased freshmen enrollment) follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate action and communication in crises
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication strategy must support and be coordinated with action components of an organizational response (Tylenol example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design an action program (stop production, establish liaison with authorities, recall product, redesign packaging, reintroduce product) and align messaging to inform, persuade, and instruct internal and external publics; centralize information release and ensure leadership visibility as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis action program elements (illustrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Action components of an effective crisis response can include: stopping production/advertising, liaising with authorities, recalling product, redesigning for safety, and returning product with assurances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete, immediate steps that remove danger and demonstrate commitment to public safety; examples from Johnson & Johnson: halted production, established liaison with police/FDA, recalled 31 million bottles, designed tamper-resistant packaging, returned product with stepped-up marketing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication objectives supporting action
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication strategy objectives: (1) inform internal and external target publics of the action; (2) persuade publics to support and accept the action; (3) possibly instruct publics in needed skills to translate intention into action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor messages to these objectives and identify specific publics, message strategy, and media strategy (e.g., gather facts, full cooperation with regulators, centralized releases, leadership appearances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions must back communication (behavior deduces purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Purposes are deduced from behavior, not rhetoric or stated goals; organizations cannot 'communicate' their way out of problems they 'behaved' into.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that communication is supported by visible, credible organizational actions; failure to act undermines message credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of coordinated action to change industry standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Action strategy can include coalition-building and standards-setting (example: buyers' coalition pushing common, verifiable food-safety standards), supported by an aggressive communication campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine collective buying power or policy changes with media outreach (op-eds, briefings) to build pressure and public support; link action (standards/agreement) with communication to achieve systemic change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick appropriate compliance-gaining strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Messages designed to shape or regulate others' behavior (compliance-gaining) may use strategies such as sanction, altruism, argument, or circumvention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the strategy suited to the goal and audience: sanction (rewards/punishments), altruism (benefit to sender/third party), argument (direct or hinted requests). Avoid circumvention (deceit/exaggeration) as unethical and damaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match persuasion vs. instruction to source power
rubrics_metrics.description: If the sender has little power or control, persuasion is the primary strategy; if the sender has power or control, instruction or direction is more relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess sender's power over receivers before selecting message tone and strategy; instructional messages fit contexts where the sender can impose or enforce behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fear appeals with efficacy and context in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Low-fear messages often produce more compliance than high-fear messages; high-fear messages combined with believable recommendations can produce high intended compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using fear appeals ensure three factors are addressed: (1) seriousness of the subject, (2) likelihood of the feared event, and (3) efficacy of the recommended action (protection motivation). Avoid high-fear without clear, believable actions for receivers to take.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose one-sided vs. two-sided arguments based on audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines: present both sides if receivers oppose your position; present one side if receivers already agree; include both sides if audience is well educated; do not omit relevant opposing arguments if using two-sided messages; use two-sided messages to inoculate audiences against later counter-arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze audience predispositions and education level; when using two-sided messages, fairly represent opposing arguments to avoid suspicion and to build resistance to counter-persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame messages for attention using 30-3-30 (or 3-30-3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Schoenfeld’s 30-3-30 formula: many give 30 seconds, some give 3 minutes, a few give 30 minutes; key points must be strong and dominantly displayed for short-attention audiences; use bold lines, subheads, illustrations for intermediate attention; provide details for long-attention audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure content at multiple levels of brevity and visual prominence to capture different audience attention spans; consider updating to a 3-30-3 model for modern contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the coorientation model when framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Know the client's/employer's position and the target publics' needs, interests, and concerns; use coorientation to determine mutual orientation and reduce discrepancies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques to reduce discrepancy include: use media identified with the audience, use highly credible sources, play down differences, seek identification in vocabulary/anecdote, establish communicator’s position as majority (from the audience itself), invoke group identifications, and modify messages to fit organizational needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — audience impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience impact: number of people affected, seriousness of consequence, directness of cause/effect, and immediacy of effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight the scale and direct consequences of an issue to increase news value for gatekeepers and audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: Proximity: the distance between the audience and the problem; local connections or angles increase news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame stories with local relevance or connections to the target audience to boost media interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Timeliness (perishability): news gets stale; journalists compete to be first and timeliness explains differences between media (broadcast vs print).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide timely angles and recognize that different media prioritize different aspects (when vs why/how); act quickly to capitalize on news windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — prominence
rubrics_metrics.description: Prominence: recognizable and well-known people/organizations attract interest; journalists and audiences focus on public figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage spokespeople or notable figures when appropriate to raise story salience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — novelty or oddity
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty/oddity: the unusual, bizarre, deviant, or offbeat attracts attention; news often defined as deviation from the normal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize unique or unexpected elements to increase media pickup, while ensuring relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — conflict, drama, or excitement
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict, drama, or excitement (strikes, disputes, crime, politics, sports) are major ingredients in news selection because of audience appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and responsibly frame conflict or dramatic elements without sensationalism; recognize journalists’ tendency to prefer such angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make messages understandable and immediately actionable
rubrics_metrics.description: Messages for media consumption must be uncomplicated, free of jargon, topical or local, and immediately actionable (provide information that empowers the audience to act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid jargon, provide clear answers to audience questions and include mobilizing information (identification, location, instruction) because journalists often omit such details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include mobilizing information when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Mobilizing information (identification, location, instruction/direction) tells audience members how to act; journalists systematically tend to shy away from including this in stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When public action is a goal, incorporate explicit mobilizing details in communications or supplementary materials because news stories may omit them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider priming and prior reputation effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Priming: previously learned information affects receptivity and interpretation of new messages; conditioning effect of prior reputation influences how audiences interpret later actions (good reputation leads to positive inferences; bad reputation triggers suspicion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and, if necessary, work to enhance intrinsic trustworthiness and reputation before attempting prosocial influence; tailor frames considering what issues are currently salient to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for audience social context and media communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Four facts: (1) audiences live within social institutions and multiple influences, (2) people selectively consume media aligned with their views, (3) media form separate communities with distinct audiences, (4) media effects vary and include unintended consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment audiences by social context and media preferences; pick channels and frames aligned with those communities; anticipate both intended and unintended effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure accurate encoding and decoding
rubrics_metrics.description: Encoding is putting meaning into messages; decoding is getting meaning out. The effective practitioner creates messages to facilitate accurate decoding and avoid miscommunication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design messages with audience decoding in mind—test for likely interpretations, simplify where necessary, and plan follow-up to correct misinterpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master semantics — word choice, denotation, connotation, and translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must seek mastery of word meanings and nuances; be aware of denotative vs connotative meanings and of translation pitfalls (examples: census Spanish tagline, historical translation errors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose words carefully, test translations with target communities, avoid ambiguous terms with conflicting connotations, and be mindful that small lexical choices can have major consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use symbols and logos with cultural sensitivity and distinctiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols compress complex meanings and can create instant recognition (e.g., Smokey Bear, Red Cross), but symbols must be distinct, in character, and decoded as intended across cultures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure symbols are culturally appropriate, monitor shifting public climates that may render symbols offensive, and involve relevant stakeholders (e.g., tribes) when symbols touch sensitive identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of stereotypes and constructed public images
rubrics_metrics.description: People hold mental images and stereotypes derived from fragmentary sources; public personalities are shaped by images fixed in the public imagination which may differ from private reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize how stereotypes and preexisting images will influence decoding; craft messages that either work with or deliberately reframe those images, using evidence and consistent behavior to shift perceptions.
